archetype.name: Retooling (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A team climbing out of a bottom-of-the-league season on the back of a defense that already plays like a good one, while the offense and the protection are still a work in progress.

report.headline: A league-average team now, held back by sacks, flags and a dead run game
report.take:
Last year's Jets ranked last in the league in net EPA and point differential and went 3-14. This year's version sits 18th in net EPA at 0.003, essentially a break-even team, and the 2-4 record is about what the scoring margin says it should be. Wins over expected is only -0.32, so this is not an unlucky team waiting for a correction. It is a middling team that has lost to Green Bay, Detroit, Chicago and New England and beaten Tennessee and Cleveland. The Book has been slow to catch up: the Jets have covered at a 0.8 clip, second in the league.

The defense drives it. It ranks 11th in EPA allowed and 7th in points allowed at 20.3 a game, built on a run defense that is 4th in rush EPA allowed. It also tackles cleanly, with the 3rd-best missed-tackle rate, and finishes plays at the quarterback, with 17 sacks for 5th in the league. The pass defense is softer, 19th in pass EPA allowed and 22nd in success rate allowed. It gives up a steady stream of completions underneath rather than big plays, and the low points total comes partly from red-zone stops, where it ranks 7th.

The offense is the problem. Geno Smith's passing has been decent in aggregate, 17th in pass EPA. It has also swung wildly: +10.9 at Detroit, then -4.9 at Chicago and -11.3 against Cleveland. Two structural issues hold it down. The first is protection: a 9.2% sack rate, 30th, with 19 sacks taken, even though the pressure rate allowed is middle of the pack. That suggests holding the ball and failing to escape as much as losing up front. The second is the run game, 23rd in rush EPA with a stuff rate of 25%. The Jets lean run anyway, with a pass rate over expected of -3.4, which caps the ceiling. On top of that come 8.7 penalties a game, 28th, including 156 penalty yards in the three-point loss to Green Bay.

The turnover margin is positive, but the defense's takeaway count is only 13th, so this is not a record propped up by takeaways. What should change is the schedule. Two games against winless Miami and one against winless LA are still to come, which gives this team a real path to respectability. The run of KC, Buffalo twice, Denver and Minnesota means a winning record is unlikely.

strengths.title: Run defense that shuts down ground games
strengths.body: The Jets are 4th in rush EPA allowed and hold lead backs well under their usual production. A sure-tackling front explains much of it, with the league's 3rd-best missed-tackle rate. Chicago ran for 232 on them, so it isn't airtight. Still, it is the most reliable part of the team and it fits a coaching staff whose identity is defense.

strengths.title: Pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: Seventeen sacks ranks 5th, and the sack rate of 7.7% is 6th. That is despite a pressure rate that is only 15th, so the rush converts pressure into sacks at a high clip. The total is inflated by an 8-sack day against Cleveland, and the defense was shut out of sacks at New England. Expect the conversion rate to drift down somewhat.

strengths.title: Points defense that bends, not breaks
strengths.body: They allow 20.3 points a game, 7th, and hold red-zone TDs to 50%, also 7th, while allowing an above-average success rate. Some of that red-zone efficiency will regress. The run defense underneath it is real, though, and that keeps the scoring defense in the top third.

concerns.title: Sacks killing drives
concerns.body: A 9.2% sack rate ranks 30th, and the Jets have taken at least three sacks in five of six games. The pressure rate allowed is only 17th, so this is as much about the quarterback holding the ball as about the line. With guard Dylan Parham out, it is unlikely to improve soon. It is the single biggest drag on an offense that otherwise passes at an average level.

concerns.title: A run game they lean on anyway
concerns.body: Rush EPA ranks 23rd, the stuff rate is 26th and yards before contact is 24th. That points to the line not winning up front, not the backs failing. The Jets still run more than expected, which keeps games close but keeps scoring low, at 18.7 points a game for 27th. With Breece Hall out, Braelon Allen carries the load alone.

concerns.title: Penalties and volatility
concerns.body: At 8.7 penalties a game, 28th, the Jets give back field position they can't afford with a low-scoring offense. The Green Bay loss carried 156 penalty yards. Combined with passing that ranged from very good to very bad week to week, the margin for error in one-score games is thin. That shows in their 0.25 win rate in those games.

trend.note: The defense has been steady from week to week, but the passing game has swung from +10.9 EPA at Detroit to -11.3 against Cleveland. Results have tracked the opponent: they beat the weak teams and played the good ones close without winning.

nextGame.headline: Winless Miami's leaky pass defense should give Geno room
nextGame.body:
Miami is the worst team in the league by net EPA and point differential, and the matchup tilts the Jets' way on both sides. The Dolphins' pass defense is 31st in EPA allowed, they have generated only 4 sacks, and they allow 51.7% on third down. That relieves the Jets' biggest problem, sacks, and their passing should play up. On the other side, Malik Willis leads a run-heavy offense, 31st in pass rate over expected, straight into a Jets run defense that ranks 4th. Miami's line also allows the 31st-ranked pressure rate. The Book has the Jets -4.5 with a 38.5 total, a low-scoring game the home team should control.

The Jets will be without guard Dylan Parham, back Breece Hall, receiver Adonai Mitchell and edge Joseph Ossai. The thin line and receiving corps raise the risk of the same stalled drives. Miami's secondary is battered: safety Michael Taaffe and corners JuJu Brents and Reese Taylor are questionable, and Storm Duck was ruled out the prior week. Receiver Caleb Douglas and guard Jonah Savaiinaea are limited. Whatever coverage Miami can field matters most against a team that wants to throw on it.

waysToWin.title: Throw on a broken pass defense
waysToWin.body: Miami is 31st in pass EPA allowed and last in sack rate, and its secondary is banged up. The Jets' passing is roughly average when it isn't being sacked. This is the week the pocket should hold, and Garrett Wilson and the short game can move the chains.

waysToWin.title: Feed the tight end
waysToWin.body: Miami has been the worst team in the league at covering tight ends by EPA per play, and tight ends score well over their usual fantasy output against it. Kenyon Sadiq is second on the team in targets. Miami's WR1 numbers in fantasy points are strong, but by EPA per play they are weak, so funneling targets to the middle of the field is the cleanest path.

waysToWin.title: Make Willis throw under pressure
waysToWin.body: Miami runs far more than expected because it can't pass, and the Jets' run defense ranks 4th. Take the run away and the Dolphins must drop back behind a line that allows the 31st-ranked pressure rate. That plays into a Jets rush that converts pressure into sacks.

waysToLose.title: Sacks and flags stall the offense
waysToLose.body: Even against Cleveland the Jets took four sacks, turned it over twice and posted -11.3 passing EPA, winning only because the defense dominated. With Parham out, a repeat of that sloppiness keeps a 38.5-total game within reach for Miami.

waysToLose.title: No ground game without Hall
waysToLose.body: The Jets' run game is 23rd in EPA, but Miami's run defense is a respectable 13th, and Hall is out. If the Jets keep running at their usual rate into a front that holds up, drives die and the game stays tight into the fourth quarter, where they are 0.25 in one-score games.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Jets' sack count stays low against the league's weakest pass rush. If Geno is still going down three or four times against Miami, the protection problem is the quarterback's as much as the line's.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense looks sustainable. Run defense and tackling are stable traits, though the sack conversion and red-zone stops will likely ease a little. The offense should stay below average unless the sack rate falls, and the run game shows no sign of fixing itself with Hall out. The Jets have covered at a 0.8 clip; that rate will fall as the Book adjusts to the fact that this team is no longer last year's. The schedule is split: Miami twice, winless LA and Arizona are winnable, while KC, Buffalo twice, Denver, New England and Minnesota are hard. Las Vegas is a coin flip.

Expect a team that hovers around .500 the rest of the way. That likely lands somewhere in the six-to-eight-win range, a clear step up from 3-14, but probably short of the playoff race in a division with Buffalo and New England ahead.

confidence.note: Six games; the defense profile is consistent, but offensive results swing widely and several starters are out.
